title: Microstructural Generative Inverse Models for Additive Manufacturing Digital Twins
authors: Pablo Luna Falcon, Jason Mayeur, Amirkoushyar Ziabari, Vincent Paquit, Patxi Fernandez-Zelaia
abstract: Metal additive manufacturing (AM) offers substantial advantages to the fabrication of complex structural components, but its widespread adoption is slowed due to complexities in the process-structure-property relations which is the cause for uncertainty and drives risk. Accurately quantifying these complex relations solely via experimental workflows is time consuming and costly. Integrated computational materials and engineering (ICME) frameworks address this challenge by leveraging advanced computational tools, such as crystal plasticity finite element models (CPFEM), to predict critical mechanical properties directly from microstructural data. However, these frameworks require a large datasets that are often difficult to obtain, and their predictive accuracy depends on the availability of realistic AM microstructure representations. Generative deep learning models are a promising approach towards synthesizing AM microstructures which contain complex morphological and crystallographic features. Denoising diffusion probabilistic models (DDPMs), in particular, show a strong potential to capture the inherent complexities of AM structures. In this work, we demonstrate that DDPMs can reliably synthesize digital-twin orientation-imaging micrographs, and we support this claim with quantitative evidence of the fidelity of the generated samples. Additionally, we establish a classifier-free guidance framework for solving complex inverse problems such as property-to-structure and process-to-structure mappings, and we showcase a potential application on a qualification-relevant uncertainty quantification problem. Our work highlights the potential of AI-based generative modeling as a key component of computational frameworks for accelerating AM materials qualification and certification.

infographic.key_insight: Denoising diffusion models generate realistic additive-manufacturing microstructure images and enable inverse mappings from target properties or process conditions to microstructures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Generative microstructure models could support CPFEM-based digital twins and uncertainty quantification to accelerate metal AM qualification.
method: Train denoising diffusion probabilistic models to synthesize orientation-imaging micrographs.
Use classifier-free guidance for property-to-structure and process-to-structure inverse mappings.
Demonstrate a qualification-relevant uncertainty quantification application.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports quantitative evidence of generated-sample fidelity but provides no dataset sizes, evaluation metrics, or numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Image fidelity alone does not establish mechanical predictive accuracy; generated microstructures need validation in downstream CPFEM workflows.
infographic.paper_title: Microstructural Generative Inverse Models for Additive Manufacturing Digital Twins

title: Scalable Stress-Constrained Topology Optimization: A Super-resolution and Simultaneous Approach Based on Machine Learning
authors: Xiangyu Sun, Shirin Hosseinmardi, Ramin Bostanabad
abstract: Large-scale topology optimization (TO) remains computationally demanding, especially for stress-constrained problems. To address this challenge, we propose the simultaneous neural topology optimization (SNTO) framework where we represent state, adjoint, and design variables with custom neural networks (NNs) whose parameters are jointly optimized within a single optimization loop that leverages continuous adjoint analysis and automatic differentiation. This optimization minimizes a multi-component loss function that combines the design objective, an aggregation of the local stress constraints, and the potential energy functionals. Our NNs have a unique architecture that accelerates convergence while enabling the networks to capture sharp gradients and boundaries which are critical to stress-constrained TO. To achieve scalability to millions of degrees of freedom (DoF), we develop a hardware-aware training scheme in which the design domain is partitioned into subdomains that are distributed across multiple GPUs. To control peak GPU memory usage, we further slice each subdomain into smaller regions whose loss gradients are evaluated sequentially and accumulated to update the NN parameters. Unlike domain decomposition approaches, our partitioning naturally ensures field continuity across the subdomains and does not require the introduction of additional terms into the loss function. For validation, we first evaluate the proposed framework on various 2D stress-constrained benchmarks and compare our results to a conventional finite element-based approach, showing that SNTO produces super-resolution designs with sharper boundaries, smaller gray areas, and lower volume fractions. We then consider large-scale 3D problems with up to eight million collocation points and distribute the training over up to eight GPUs.

infographic.key_insight: Simultaneous neural topology optimization jointly optimizes state, adjoint, and design fields to produce scalable, super-resolution stress-constrained designs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework targets material-efficient structural design under stress limits while scaling computation across multiple GPUs.
method: Represent state, adjoint, and design variables with custom neural networks optimized in a single loop.
Combine the design objective, aggregated local stress constraints, and potential energy functionals using continuous adjoints and automatic differentiation.
Distribute domain partitions across GPUs and accumulate gradients over smaller slices to control peak memory without additional interface loss terms.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports sharper boundaries, smaller gray areas, and lower volume fractions than a conventional FEM-based approach on 2D benchmarks, plus 3D demonstrations with up to eight million collocation points on eight GPUs.
infographic.watch_item: Aggregated stress constraints warrant checking local stress peaks; the abstract does not quantify constraint accuracy or runtime gains.
infographic.paper_title: Scalable Stress-Constrained Topology Optimization: A Super-resolution and Simultaneous Approach Based on Machine Learning

title: Synthetic Dataset Generation, Physical Consistency and Active Learning for Shape-Informed Surrogate Modeling of Hemodynamics
authors: Francesco Romor, Richard Schussnig, Charles A. Taylor, Gerhard A. Holzapfel, Alfonso Caiazzo
abstract: Model order reduction has the potential to enable real-time patient-specific assessment of cardiovascular flows. However, it still faces significant challenges stemming from the geometric variability of vascular anatomies. Building upon the SynthAorta dataset (Bosnjak et al., IEEE Trans. Med. Imag. 45(1), 2026) of physiological aortic geometries, we generate an extensive dataset of physiologically consistent computational fluid dynamics solutions through an automatic boundary-condition adjustment procedure. A common reference geometry allows all patient-specific anatomies to be represented by displacement fields, providing point-to-point correspondence without the need for geometric registration. Based on this dataset, we develop Graph U-Net and Transformer U-Net surrogate models to predict velocity and pressure fields at peak systole. We further investigate two strategies to enhance data efficiency and prediction accuracy: active learning and differentiable physical consistency constraints based on the finite element residual. The results show that active learning is strongly regime-dependent: while it offers little benefit over random sampling during early training, it improves performance during fine-tuning through gradient- and subspace-based acquisition strategies. Similarly, physical consistency constraints prove to be substantially more effective as a fine-tuning objective than as a regularizer applied throughout training. Finally, out-of-distribution studies demonstrate that the primary limitation of surrogate models lies in the geometric support of the underlying parametrization rather than in the neural network architectures themselves. The proposed framework combines synthetic dataset generation, geometry-aware surrogate modeling, physics-informed optimization, and active learning into a scalable workflow for inter-patient hemodynamic prediction.

infographic.key_insight: For shape-informed hemodynamic surrogates, active learning and finite-element physical consistency are more effective during fine-tuning than during initial training.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The workflow supports scalable prediction of patient-specific aortic velocity and pressure fields, advancing surrogate modeling toward rapid cardiovascular assessment.
method: Generate physiologically consistent CFD data from SynthAorta geometries using automatic boundary-condition adjustment.
Represent anatomies as displacement fields on a common reference geometry and train Graph U-Net and Transformer U-Net surrogates.
Fine-tune with active learning and differentiable finite-element residual constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: Peak-systolic field evaluations show fine-tuning benefits from gradient- and subspace-based acquisition, while out-of-distribution tests identify geometric coverage as the primary limitation.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization remains limited by the geometric support of the anatomy parametrization; changing network architecture alone may not resolve this.
infographic.paper_title: Synthetic Dataset Generation, Physical Consistency and Active Learning for Shape-Informed Surrogate Modeling of Hemodynamics

title: Robust topology optimization of isogeometric Kirchhoff--Love shells by the Speed Method
authors: Philipp Eisenhardt, Fernando Hübner Scherer, Barbara Wohlmuth, Andrei Constantinescu
abstract: This paper presents a framework for robust topology optimization of Kirchhoff-Love (KL) multi-patch shells using isogeometric analysis and non-matching meshes and provides a CAD-compatible method. The material distribution is optimized via a NURBS-based level set method, enabling accurate boundary representation and seamless export to standard CAD/CAM workflows. The shape derivative is computed using the speed method, yielding a volume-based formulation that avoids boundary approximations and aligns with the isogeometric principle of coarse, high-order discretizations. This eliminates the need for local refinement, adaptive quadrature, or trimming as the descent direction for the compliance and volume objectives are obtained through a biharmonic equation. The framework is extended to robust optimization under uncertainty, accounting for stochastic loading and material properties via Monte Carlo sampling and Gaussian Random Fields. Numerical examples demonstrate the method's efficiency and robustness across single- and multi-patch shells, reproducing literature results with fewer elements than traditional FEM or refined IGA approaches. The developed methods and tools can be directly extended to problems involving stress-based optimization and risk-averse metrics. The numerical implementations are open-source and available on GitHub.

infographic.key_insight: A NURBS level-set framework enables robust, CAD-compatible topology optimization of isogeometric Kirchhoff–Love shells using volume-based shape derivatives.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports lightweight shell design under uncertain loads and material properties while preserving compatibility with CAD/CAM workflows.
method: Model single- and multi-patch shells with isogeometric analysis, including non-matching meshes.
Use the speed method and a biharmonic equation to obtain descent directions without local refinement, adaptive quadrature, or trimming.
Represent uncertainty through Monte Carlo sampling and Gaussian random fields.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical examples reproduce literature results with fewer elements than traditional FEM or refined IGA approaches, although the abstract provides no quantitative speedup.
infographic.watch_item: Monte Carlo sampling may increase optimization cost; fewer elements alone do not establish lower total runtime.
infographic.paper_title: Robust topology optimization of isogeometric Kirchhoff--Love shells by the Speed Method

title: Hyperreduction accelerates finite element model updating for the discovery of neural materials
authors: Hagen Holthusen, Matthias Knipper, Kevin Linka
abstract: Finite element model updating is among the most general approaches to discover constitutive models from structural experiments: since the displacement field is computed rather than measured, it accommodates arbitrary geometries, boundary conditions, and sparse or noisy data. However, every loss evaluation requires a nonlinear finite element solve per load step, and training neural materials requires many such evaluations. Intrusive model order reduction lowers this cost while retaining boundary conditions and variational structure. How can a reduced model remain accurate while the network weights change at every training step? We combine proper orthogonal decomposition and energy-conserving sampling and weighting with adjoint sensitivities of the reduced model, and adapt both the trial space and the sampled elements along the optimization path. The constitutive law is a polyconvex neural network: a logarithmic normalization term, together with a zero-anchored input convex architecture and a growth term, renders the energy polyconvex, coercive, and non-negative by construction, independent of the trained weights. We demonstrate the approach on two experimental datasets and one synthetic three-dimensional example. For a two-phase specimen, training time decreases from nine hours to 41 minutes compared with a full-order identification, without loss of accuracy. In the three-dimensional example, six modes replace 48 672 degrees of freedom, 116 of 15 625 elements suffice to evaluate the internal forces, and training takes 13 minutes. In all cases, the identified material reproduces the measured reaction force and predicts the displacement field from the force alone. Hyperreduction makes the discovery of neural materials from structural data affordable while retaining the advantages of finite element model updating.

infographic.key_insight: Adaptive hyperreduction accelerates finite element discovery of neural constitutive laws while preserving accuracy as network weights change.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can identify material behavior from structural reaction-force data without requiring measured full-field displacements, while accommodating arbitrary geometries and boundary conditions.
method: Combine proper orthogonal decomposition with energy-conserving sampling and weighting.
Adapt the reduced trial space and sampled elements during training using reduced-model adjoint sensitivities.
Use a neural energy architecture that guarantees polyconvexity, coercivity, and non-negativity by construction.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across two experimental datasets and one synthetic 3D example, the method reproduced reaction forces and predicted displacement fields; two-phase training fell from nine hours to 41 minutes without reported accuracy loss.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy depends on adapting the reduced basis and element sampling as the constitutive model evolves during optimization.
infographic.paper_title: Hyperreduction accelerates finite element model updating for the discovery of neural materials

title: Elastic theory of ideal liquid crystal elastomers
authors: Zumrat Usmanova, Ruobing Bai
abstract: A liquid crystal elastomer (LCE) exhibits a two-way coupling between its mesogen order and network elasticity: the mesogen order sets the undeformed network conformation, and the network deformation reorients the mesogens. This coupling gives rise to large, reversible stimuli-responsive actuation, as well as to soft elasticity, a finite deformation at nearly zero stress. This article reviews the elastic theory of ideal LCEs, bridging single-chain statistics and continuum constitutive models. The "ideal" elastic behavior rests on the assumption of anisotropic Gaussian chains that retain no memory of the crosslinking state, such that rotating the director costs no free energy. The corresponding neo-classical free energy of a monodomain LCE is non-quasi-convex, with a continuous family of stress-free ground states, leading to thermally induced spontaneous deformation and soft elasticity accommodated by coexisting stripe domains. The quasi-convex relaxation of the free energy classifies the behavior of polydomain LCEs into three phases, each with a distinct macroscopic mechanical response depending on the stretch state. The ideal elastic theory can be further extended to incorporate additional behaviors and physical processes, including thermo- and photomechanical coupling, Frank elasticity from director distortion, semi-soft or non-soft behavior arising from network nonideality, and temperature- and rate-dependent viscoelasticity.

infographic.key_insight: Ideal liquid crystal elastomers couple mesogen orientation and network deformation, enabling reversible actuation and finite deformation at nearly zero stress.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The theory provides a constitutive foundation for modeling soft actuators and predicting stretch-dependent mechanical responses in liquid crystal elastomers.
method: Bridge anisotropic Gaussian chain statistics with neo-classical continuum elasticity.
Explain spontaneous deformation and soft elasticity through stress-free states and coexisting stripe domains.
Use quasi-convex energy relaxation to classify polydomain behavior into three mechanical phases.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a theoretical review and three-phase classification, but reports no experimental datasets or quantitative validation metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Ideal behavior assumes no memory of the crosslinking state; realistic predictions may require nonideality, director-gradient, and viscoelastic contributions.
infographic.paper_title: Elastic theory of ideal liquid crystal elastomers

title: Peridynamic Thermo-Mechanical Modeling of Cracking in Tungsten under Fusion-Relevant Heat Fluxes
authors: Rinkle Juneja, Pablo Seleson, Samuel Temple Reeve, Justin Weinmeister, Gary Staebler
abstract: Plasma-facing materials (PFMs) are the primary armor materials in fusion reactors, protecting reactor wall components from extreme heat fluxes, energetic particles, and intense neutron irradiation. These harsh conditions induce thermo-mechanical stresses, irradiation damage, and overall degradation in PFMs. Among these, thermo-mechanical damage induced by extreme heat flux is one of the key factors limiting the lifetime of PFMs. We present a modeling and simulation approach for predicting thermo-mechanical cracking and damage in tungsten, a leading PFM candidate, under fusion-reactor-relevant heat fluxes. Specifically, we study damage induced by cyclic electron beam (e-beam) exposure under different combinations of base temperature and heat flux. We carry out component-scale thermo-mechanical simulations using CabanaPD, a peridynamics fracture mechanics code, informed by experimental data for recrystallized pure tungsten from the JUDITH e-beam facility. The simulations compare well with the experimental classification and enable identification of cracking thresholds across a range of heat fluxes and base temperatures. These predictions can provide detailed insights into the spatial distribution and temporal accumulation of cracks and damage, while offering a pathway for screening candidate PFMs and quantifying their lifespan under fusion-relevant conditions.

infographic.key_insight: Peridynamic thermo-mechanical simulations predict cracking thresholds in tungsten under cyclic, fusion-relevant heat fluxes across different base temperatures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a pathway to screen plasma-facing materials and assess heat-flux-driven damage that limits fusion-component lifetime.
method: Run component-scale thermo-mechanical fracture simulations using CabanaPD.
Model cyclic electron-beam exposure across base temperatures and heat fluxes.
Track the spatial distribution and temporal accumulation of cracks and damage.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations informed by JUDITH electron-beam experiments on recrystallized pure tungsten agree well with experimental damage classifications.
infographic.watch_item: Validation described in the abstract concerns electron-beam-induced thermal damage, not the combined particle and neutron exposure of a fusion reactor.
infographic.paper_title: Peridynamic Thermo-Mechanical Modeling of Cracking in Tungsten under Fusion-Relevant Heat Fluxes

title: HERD: Harness-Evolving Recursive Distillation for Continual Learning
authors: Xun Sun, Thanh Thi Nguyen, Thuy-Trang Vu
abstract: Continual learning requires a model to keep acquiring new skills and knowledge without compromising its existing capabilities. Parametric methods suffer from catastrophic forgetting and loss of plasticity. Non-parametric methods, such as prompts, skills, and harnesses, leverage in-context learning but are limited by context length and lossy plain-text compression. To effectively combine their complementary strengths, we propose HERD (Harness-Evolving Recursive Distillation), a hybrid continual learning framework that learns efficiently in the harness and internalizes experience into cumulative capabilities via distillation. On the harness side, HERD continually refines its skills to capture reusable patterns, while retaining high-residual examples that the skills fail to capture in a bounded memory. On the parameter side, HERD performs drift-constrained distillation with dual anchors, substantially reducing forgetting over long recursive runs. On the 25-stage task stream of TRACE+17, under fixed memory and compute budgets, HERD matches the strongest parametric baseline in new-task acquisition while exhibiting the least forgetting and the strongest retention of general capabilities.

infographic.key_insight: HERD combines an evolving external harness with recursive distillation to acquire new capabilities while limiting catastrophic forgetting.
infographic.engineering_relevance: HERD could support continually updated engineering AI assistants, but the abstract provides no solid-mechanics or constitutive-modeling validation.
method: Refine reusable skills in an external harness.
Retain high-residual examples in bounded memory.
Distill experience into model parameters using dual-anchor drift constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the 25-stage TRACE+17 task stream under fixed memory and compute budgets, HERD matches the strongest parametric baseline in new-task acquisition while reporting the least forgetting and strongest general-capability retention.
infographic.watch_item: Transfer to mechanics applications remains untested in the abstract; retention of physical consistency would require separate evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: HERD: Harness-Evolving Recursive Distillation for Continual Learning

title: A high-order multi-scale method and its error analysis for nonlocal-in-time fractionally damped wave problems in composite materials
authors: Gehao Wang, Hao Dong, Yufeng Nie, Junzhi Cui
abstract: Significant spatial heterogeneity and nonlocal history-dependent attenuation jointly govern wave propagation in composite materials, making full-scale direct numerical simulation (DNS) computationally prohibitive. This study proposed a high-order multi-scale (HOMS) method for nonlocal-in-time fractionally damped wave problems with highly oscillatory and discontinuous material coefficients. Using a multi-scale asymptotic expansion approach, the macroscopic homogenized equation, and first- and second-order correction terms are derived to construct the high-accuracy HOMS solution. Moreover, a local pointwise error analysis identifies the leading residual eliminated by this HOMS solution and validates its local physical balance preservation. Then, a global energy-norm error estimate establishes the $O(\varepsilon)$-order convergence rate for the HOMS solution. Subsequently, an efficient spatiotemporal multi-scale algorithm integrating the finite element and finite difference methods is designed, which employs a novel fully discrete $L2\text{-}1_σ$-Newmark scheme, and corresponding unconditional shifted-energy stability and explicit convergence rates are also obtained for the macroscopic homogenized displacement and velocity, respectively. Both two- and three-dimensional examples are presented to demonstrate the accuracy, efficiency, reduced cost, and robustness of the proposed HOMS method. This work provides an effective multi-scale tool for nonlocal-in-time wave simulation in engineering applications.

infographic.key_insight: A high-order multiscale method captures heterogeneous, fractionally damped wave propagation with an O(ε) global energy-norm error estimate.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method reduces the computational burden of simulating history-dependent wave attenuation in composite materials compared with full-scale direct numerical simulation.
method: Derive a homogenized wave equation and first- and second-order corrections through multiscale asymptotic expansion.
Establish local residual cancellation, global error bounds, and unconditional shifted-energy stability.
Combine finite elements and finite differences using a fully discrete L2-1σ–Newmark scheme.
infographic.evidence_signal: Two- and three-dimensional numerical examples demonstrate accuracy, efficiency, reduced cost, and robustness, although the abstract reports no quantitative benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Fractional damping requires history-dependent calculations; the abstract does not specify long-time memory costs or history-compression strategies.
infographic.paper_title: A high-order multi-scale method and its error analysis for nonlocal-in-time fractionally damped wave problems in composite materials

title: Conservative Finite Element Methods for Kirchhoff-Type Equations
authors: Benjamin Dörich, Felix Krumbiegel, Jemal Rogava, Andreas Rupp, Zurab Vashakidze
abstract: We construct and analyse a fully discrete scheme for a Kirchhoff-type nonlinear integro-differential equation in two spatial dimensions with time-dependent coefficients. The scheme combines a symmetric three-layer time discretization of Crank--Nicolson type with a conforming finite element method of arbitrary polynomial degree $p$ and a Picard iteration for the nonlinearity. We prove that the Picard iteration is well defined and, that the iterates converge to the Ritz projection of the exact solution measured in fractional-power norms of the discrete Laplacian. Running the same energy argument in the unshifted norms, and under the same hypotheses, we then obtain the optimal order $\mathcal{O} ( h^{p+1} + τ^2 )$ in $L^2$ and $\mathcal{O} ( h^{p} + τ^2 )$ in $H^1$ for the full error. For the homogeneous problem with constant coefficients, the exact solution of the scheme moreover preserves a discrete energy identically. Numerical experiments with manufactured solutions reproduce the predicted second order in time and the full spatial order $h^{p+1}$ in the $L^2$-norm.

infographic.key_insight: A fully discrete finite element scheme for Kirchhoff-type equations achieves optimal spatial accuracy and second-order time accuracy, while preserving discrete energy for homogeneous problems with constant coefficients.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports accurate simulation of nonlocal nonlinear structural dynamics where energy consistency helps control numerical artifacts.
method: Conforming finite elements of arbitrary polynomial degree p in two spatial dimensions.
Symmetric three-layer Crank–Nicolson-type time discretization.
Picard iteration for the nonlinearity, with convergence and error analysis.
infographic.evidence_signal: Manufactured-solution experiments reproduce second-order temporal convergence and spatial L² convergence of order h^(p+1), consistent with the theoretical error bounds.
infographic.watch_item: Exact discrete energy preservation is established only for the homogeneous, constant-coefficient problem; the general convergence results require the paper’s stated hypotheses.
infographic.paper_title: Conservative Finite Element Methods for Kirchhoff-Type Equations

title: Can Language Models Get "Aphasia" From Neuronal Ablation?
authors: Pratik Worah, Randall Bateman
abstract: Progressive neuronal loss is the hallmark of neurodegenerative disease, yet how loss of neurons shapes the pattern of cognitive decline remains poorly understood. Here we systematically ablate neurons (computational units) in language models spanning recurrent long short-term memory (LSTM) and Transformer architectures and apply limited fine-tuning as a simple proxy for compensatory plasticity. With whole-unit ablation, LSTMs degrade gradually with syntactic and semantic faculties declining in parallel across mild-to-moderate damage. By contrast, Transformers exhibit late threshold-like collapse under feedforward multi-layer perceptron (MLP) ablation and smoother sigmoid-like decline under attention-head ablation. Qualitatively, MLP-ablated models continue to make within-category semantic substitutions (semantic paraphasias) alongside rising non-responses, paralleling Wernicke-type aphasia, while attention-head ablation produces a trend toward loss of semantic specificity similar to the semantic variant of primary progressive aphasia (svPPA). These findings indicate that feedforward and attentional pathways have functionally distinct failure modes, suggesting that architecture-dependent failure profiles may offer new computational perspectives on aphasic syndromes and neurodegenerative diseases as an in silico model. Notably, early accuracy retention under Transformer attention-head ablation qualitatively parallels pre-symptomatic reserve before the 40--60% neuronal loss reported by Gomez-Isla et al. (1996) when clinical symptoms emerge in Alzheimer's disease, whereas the steadier LSTM decline parallels the symptomatic progression described by DeKosky and Scheff (1990) and Terry et al. (1991).

infographic.key_insight: Neuronal ablation produces architecture-dependent language failures: gradual decline in LSTMs, threshold-like collapse from Transformer MLP damage, and smoother decline from attention-head damage.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These failure profiles offer a computational damage-tolerance perspective on how neural-network architecture influences robustness to progressive component loss.
method: Systematically ablate computational units in LSTM and Transformer language models.
Compare Transformer feedforward MLP ablation with attention-head ablation.
Apply limited fine-tuning as a proxy for compensatory plasticity.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports parallel syntactic and semantic decline in LSTMs, semantic substitutions and rising non-responses under MLP ablation, and reduced semantic specificity under attention-head ablation.
infographic.watch_item: Parallels with aphasia and neurodegeneration are qualitative; computational ablation and limited fine-tuning do not establish biological equivalence or clinical validity.
infographic.paper_title: Can Language Models Get "Aphasia" From Neuronal Ablation?

title: Generalized modeling reveals stabilizing mechanisms in cross-feeding microbial communities
authors: Tom Clegg, Thilo Gross
abstract: Understanding what makes microbial communities stable and able to resist perturbation is a fundamental question in microbial ecology. Theoretical approaches to this problem typically require making strict assumptions about the structure, parameters and functional forms used in models, hindering general insight. Here, we address this problem by developing and analyzing a generalized model of microbial community dynamics, capturing resource-mediated competitive and cross-feeding interactions between populations. The generalized modeling approach allows us to assess the stability of microbial systems across large ensembles of models with variable size, structure and non-linear dynamics. Our analysis shows how community stability is constrained by system size and identifies its key metabolic and dynamical drivers, highlighting the central roles of self-limitation, metabolic efficiency and plasticity. Furthermore, we show how the structure of communities mediates their stability, allowing communities to counteract the destabilizing cross-feeding loops through organization into hierarchical trophic structures. Together, these results provide new insight into the stability of microbial communities and offer a flexible analytical framework for future work to explore the responses of communities to perturbation.

infographic.key_insight: Microbial community stability depends on self-limitation, metabolic efficiency and plasticity, while hierarchical trophic organization can counteract destabilizing cross-feeding loops.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could inform the design of stable microbial consortia for bioprocessing, rather than AI or solid-mechanics applications.
method: Develop a generalized dynamical model of resource competition and cross-feeding.
Assess stability across large model ensembles with varying size, structure and nonlinear dynamics.
Identify metabolic, dynamical and organizational drivers of stability.
infographic.evidence_signal: Model-ensemble analysis identifies system-size constraints and stabilizing mechanisms; the abstract reports no experimental validation or quantitative performance metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Applying these insights to engineered communities requires checking model assumptions and validating stability predictions experimentally.
infographic.paper_title: Generalized modeling reveals stabilizing mechanisms in cross-feeding microbial communities

title: Mixed finite element methods for a heat-assisted model of sedimentation
authors: Julio Careaga, Cristian Inzunza
abstract: A model for the consolidation-sedimentation process incorporating thermal effects is analysed. The model is motivated by novel applications to heat-assisted sedimentation of mineral suspensions. A system of convection-diffusion equations for the concentration and temperature are coupled to flow equations for the volume-average velocity and pressure. The model is supplemented with Dirichlet and mixed boundary conditions. A quasi-stationary approach of the system is analysed by means of a mixed variational formulation, where additional variables such as the pseudostress tensor and variables for the gradient of the temperature and concentration are introduced. The existence and uniqueness of the system is shown making use of the Babu{\v s}ka-Brezzi theory and Banach's fixed-point theorem, under hypotheses of smallness of the data and additional regularity on the solutions. A discrete formulation based on finite element spaces is proposed and analysed, and the existence of solutions is achieved thanks to Brouwer's fixed-point theorem. Additionally, Céa and a priori estimates are derived for the mixed formulation. Finally, numerical examples are provided to demonstrate the performance of the model and to confirm the theoretical rates of convergence.

infographic.key_insight: A mixed finite element formulation couples heat, particle concentration, and flow to model heat-assisted consolidation and sedimentation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model supports analysis of thermal effects in mineral-suspension sedimentation, relevant to separation and thickening processes.
method: Formulate the quasi-stationary coupled system using pseudostress and temperature/concentration gradient variables.
Establish continuous well-posedness using Babuška–Brezzi theory and Banach’s fixed-point theorem.
Analyze a mixed finite element discretization, proving discrete existence and deriving Céa-type and a priori error estimates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical examples demonstrate model performance and confirm theoretical convergence rates; the abstract reports no experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: Continuous existence and uniqueness require small-data and additional solution-regularity assumptions, limiting guarantees outside those conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Mixed finite element methods for a heat-assisted model of sedimentation

title: Concurrent two-scale topology optimization of printable bone scaffolds via rectified-flow generation and exact latent-space refinement
authors: Reza T Batley, Sourav Saha
abstract: Bone scaffolds must reconcile a macroscale mechanical response with microscale geometric feasibility, yet conventional approaches to their design restrict attainable constitutive properties. This work presents a concurrent two-scale topology optimization framework; a conditional rectified flow generates periodic lattice microstructures, which are then refined in latent space by exact finite-element homogenization sensitivities. The resulting unit-cell geometries and their spatial assignments are jointly optimized under mechanical and feature-size constraints. In a distal rabbit femur benchmark, all eight flow-started refinements produce printable cells with maximum relative errors under 1\% across six prescribed engineering moduli. Constructing the implant from a single tiled cell reproduces intact whole-femur compliance within 0.1\% and regional strain energy within 0.35\% under four loading conditions. In human femoral reconstruction, multiscale concurrent optimization produces a cortical mid-shaft scaffold with porosity 63\% while satisfying the compliance constraint within 2\% under walking and stair-climbing loads. It achieves an 84\% porosity on a proximal cancellous scaffold with strain-energy deviations below 0.25\% under the same loads. Analysis of the learned representations reveals distinct architectural families in latent space. Further, the attention heads of the rectified-flow transformer specialize for spatial shifts -- learning the analogue of a finite-difference stencil -- and coordinate symmetries, with ablations showing their influence on generated topologies. These results establish a route to printable, mechanically constrained scaffold designs. The framework is general enough for extending to many other multiscale structural design applications including topology-microstructure co-design in metal additive manufacturing.

infographic.key_insight: Rectified-flow generation paired with exact latent-space refinement enables concurrent optimization of printable bone-scaffold microstructures and their spatial assignments.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework designs highly porous scaffolds that closely match target bone mechanics while enforcing mechanical and feature-size constraints.
method: Generate periodic lattice cells with a conditional rectified-flow model.
Refine cells in latent space using exact finite-element homogenization sensitivities.
Jointly optimize cell geometries and spatial assignments under mechanical and feature-size constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: Eight rabbit-benchmark refinements achieved under 1% error across six target moduli; human femoral designs reached 63% cortical porosity with compliance constraints satisfied within 2%, and 84% cancellous porosity with strain-energy deviations below 0.25%.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports computational benchmarks; fabrication accuracy, fatigue performance, and biological integration still require experimental validation.
infographic.paper_title: Concurrent two-scale topology optimization of printable bone scaffolds via rectified-flow generation and exact latent-space refinement

title: Macroscopic Nuclear Resonance Energy Transfer Mediated by Coherent Magnons
authors: Ryan Weed
abstract: Phonon-mediated nuclear Resonance Energy Transfer (RET) in metal deuterides is severely constrained by inertial rest-mass dilution, lattice fracture limits, and thermal nuclear spin cancellation. Extending the generalized nuclear Dicke model to Ferromagnetic Resonance (FMR) magnons eliminates mass dilution via hyperfine-amplified M1 coupling while unlocking relativistic Dirac M2 coupling via Overhauser spin polarization. We derive a Suhl-clamped FMR scaling law predicting 14.2 MeV (Pd-106) and 11.4 MeV (Ni-58) breakup neutrons, 19.9 MeV alpha particles, and reconciled sub-keV fusion anomalies.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes coherent magnons as mediators of nuclear resonance energy transfer, aiming to bypass mass dilution and thermal spin cancellation that constrain phonon-based approaches.
infographic.engineering_relevance: If validated, this mechanism could shift metal-deuteride design constraints from lattice fracture limits toward controlled magnetic resonance and nuclear spin polarization.
method: Extend a generalized nuclear Dicke model to ferromagnetic-resonance magnons.
Model hyperfine-amplified M1 coupling and polarization-enabled relativistic M2 coupling.
Derive a Suhl-clamped scaling law for nuclear energy transfer.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical predictions of 14.2 MeV neutrons for Pd-106, 11.4 MeV neutrons for Ni-58, and 19.9 MeV alpha particles, but describes no experimental validation.
infographic.watch_item: Experimental feasibility remains unestablished, particularly whether sufficient coherent magnon excitation and nuclear spin polarization can coexist under realistic material conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Macroscopic Nuclear Resonance Energy Transfer Mediated by Coherent Magnons

title: Finite Element Approximation of Rotating MHD-Boussinesq Flows with Nonlinear Power-Law Viscosity
authors: Akash Ashirbad Panda, Evana Islam Sarkar
abstract: We propose and analyse a fully discrete finite element approximation of the three-dimensional incompressible rotating MHD-Boussinesq system with nonlinear power-law ($p$-Laplace) viscosity. Conforming elements are used for the velocity and temperature, $\mathbf H(\operatorname{curl})$-conforming Nédélec elements for the magnetic induction, and a semi-implicit backward Euler scheme in time. The discretisation preserves the principal energy structure: the Lorentz and induction terms cancel exactly, while the Coriolis force remains energy neutral. This yields well-posedness and mesh-independent energy stability. The nonlinear power-law diffusion creates two main analytical difficulties. Since a uniform time-derivative estimate for the discrete velocity is unavailable, strong compactness is obtained through a time-translate argument and Simon's compactness criterion. The weak limit of the nonlinear diffusion is then identified by a Minty argument based on a discrete energy $\limsup$ inequality. Compactness and passage to the limit hold throughout the shear-thickening regime, while identification of a genuine weak solution is obtained in the Newtonian case and, in three dimensions, above an explicit threshold dictated by the Lorentz force rather than by convection. We further establish a priori error estimates without any mesh-time coupling condition. Three-dimensional numerical experiments confirm the stability and convergence behaviour predicted by the analysis.

infographic.key_insight: An energy-structure-preserving finite element scheme delivers mesh-independent stability for rotating MHD-Boussinesq flows with nonlinear power-law viscosity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports stable simulation of coupled flow, heat transfer, and magnetic effects in rotating electrically conducting fluids.
method: Combine conforming velocity–temperature elements, Nédélec magnetic elements, and semi-implicit backward Euler time stepping.
Preserve exact Lorentz–induction energy cancellation and energy-neutral Coriolis forcing.
Use time-translate compactness and a Minty argument to analyse convergence and identify nonlinear diffusion.
infographic.evidence_signal: Three-dimensional numerical experiments confirm predicted stability and convergence, alongside a priori error estimates requiring no mesh–time coupling.
infographic.watch_item: Genuine weak-solution identification is established only in the Newtonian case and above an explicit three-dimensional power-law threshold imposed by the Lorentz force.
infographic.paper_title: Finite Element Approximation of Rotating MHD-Boussinesq Flows with Nonlinear Power-Law Viscosity

title: Learned smoothing in operator-adapted multigrid: controlled accuracy gains and computational limits
authors: Kumar Kaushik Ranjan
abstract: Learned multigrid components are often evaluated at a fixed iteration budget, but such comparisons do not distinguish local approximation gains from practical solver efficiency. We study this distinction for high-contrast elliptic problems on unstructured finite element meshes. A learned V-cycle uses operator-dependent transfers, Galerkin coarse operators, near-kernel deflation and an energy-norm safeguard; only its smoothers are trained. The architecture represents a specified class of fixed polynomial smoothers and is positively homogeneous in the load. On fresh conductive-channel problems, one learned pass reduces the energy error by factors of 5.7-6.1 relative to the same cycle with four-step Jacobi-preconditioned conjugate-gradient smoothing; the corresponding factors are 1.38-1.45 for insulating barriers. In a separate fixed-input test on channel problems, the fine-level learned smoother attains a smaller energy-norm error than the exact minimum over a five-dimensional Krylov space of its own input on 97-100 of 100 fresh inputs for each position and training initialization; this does not establish superiority over all polynomial-smoothed cycles. When the classical smoothing budget is increased, the paired geometric-mean accuracy crosses that of the learned cycle between 8 and 14 steps per smoothing call on channels and between 5 and 8 on barriers. The measured CPU implementation offers no computational advantage over the tested classical solvers, and load changes and floating islands further restrict its accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: Learned smoothing improves energy-norm accuracy at a fixed multigrid budget, but larger classical smoothing budgets close the gap without a measured CPU advantage for learning.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For high-contrast elliptic finite element solves, fixed-budget accuracy gains should be weighed against runtime and robustness before adopting learned smoothers.
method: Train only the smoothers within an operator-adapted multigrid V-cycle.
Use operator-dependent transfers, Galerkin coarse operators, near-kernel deflation and an energy-norm safeguard.
Represent a specified class of fixed polynomial smoothers while preserving positive homogeneity in the load.
infographic.evidence_signal: On fresh problems, one learned pass reduced energy error by factors of 5.7–6.1 for conductive channels and 1.38–1.45 for insulating barriers versus the same cycle with four-step Jacobi-preconditioned CG smoothing; classical accuracy crossed the learned cycle at 8–14 and 5–8 steps per smoothing call, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: The tested CPU implementation showed no computational advantage over classical solvers, while load changes and floating islands further limited accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Learned smoothing in operator-adapted multigrid: controlled accuracy gains and computational limits

title: Geometry-Dependent Properties of Physically Crosslinked PPy-PVA Hydrogels Enable Tunable Iontophoretic Drug Delivery
authors: Heather Jin Hee Kim, Mohsen Alishahi, Kyuin Park, Mikaila K. Roncevich, Larissa M. Shepherd, Cara M. Nunez
abstract: Objective: Iontophoretic drug delivery has primarily relied on current modulation to regulate drug transport. Here, we investigate hydrogel geometry, microstructure, and local electric fields as alternative mechanisms for controlling transdermal delivery. Methods: Bovine serum albumin (BSA) was encapsulated in polypyrrole-polyvinyl alcohol (PPy-PVA) hydrogels. Five geometries, including Hilbert curve-based designs, were fabricated to vary pore architecture and local electric field distributions. We optimized PPy content, drug loading, and current density. Electric fields were evaluated using finite element analysis, and microstructures were characterized by scanning electron microscopy. Drug transport was assessed using Franz diffusion cells with artificial membranes. Results: Hydrogel geometries exhibited distinct microstructures and electric field distributions. Iontophoresis substantially enhanced permeability compared with passive diffusion, while individual geometries produced different cumulative release, flux, and permeability profiles. The average iontophoretic permeability was (3.80 +/- 1.93) x 10^-5, exceeding previously reported values using artificial membranes. Conclusion: Geometry-driven fabrication of drug-loaded hydrogels enables tunable transport characteristics under both iontophoretic and passive conditions. Significance: Geometry-mediated control offers an alternative approach to regulating iontophoretic drug delivery without requiring individual current-density modulation.

infographic.key_insight: PPy-PVA hydrogel geometry provides an additional lever for tuning drug transport by altering microstructure and local electric fields.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Geometry-driven hydrogel design could enable tunable iontophoretic delivery without separately adjusting current density for each design.
method: Fabricated BSA-loaded hydrogels in five geometries, including Hilbert curve-based designs.
Evaluated electric fields with finite element analysis and microstructure with scanning electron microscopy.
Measured passive and iontophoretic transport using Franz diffusion cells with artificial membranes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The five geometries showed distinct release, flux, and permeability profiles; average iontophoretic permeability was (3.80 ± 1.93) × 10⁻⁵, with units unspecified in the abstract.
infographic.watch_item: Artificial-membrane testing does not establish performance or safety in skin, and the abstract reports no AI surrogate model.
infographic.paper_title: Geometry-Dependent Properties of Physically Crosslinked PPy-PVA Hydrogels Enable Tunable Iontophoretic Drug Delivery

title: VecTile: A Low-Cost Flexible Tactile Array for 3-DoF Force Sensing
authors: Jian Hou, Xin Zhou, Adam J. Spiers
abstract: Tactile sensing provides robots with contact information difficult to obtain from vision alone. Shear force is particularly important for understanding tangential contact, guiding corrective motions, and maintaining grasp stability, yet flexible and low-cost tactile arrays often measure only normal force. We introduce VecTile, a low-cost, 6 mm thin, flexible tactile array capable of three-axis force sensing. VecTile combines a piezoresistive layer with passive silicone nubs that convert normal and shear forces into distinguishable pressure patterns. The sensor can be fabricated in-house without specialized equipment. The complete system costs less than 35 USD for a 4x4 array. We validate the sensing mechanism through finite element analysis and hardware experiments. In controlled single-taxel tests over 1-5 N normal force and up to 1.5 N shear force, VecTile achieves root-mean-square errors of 0.39 N and 0.16 N for normal and shear forces. A VecTile calibrated while flat retains accuracy when curved, while a five-minute manual calibration is sufficient for practical use. Two applications demonstrate its utility. First, shear readings are sensitive enough to stop a sharp scalpel from puncturing a balloon after contact. Second, the sensor substantially improves Diffusion Policy-guided power-plug insertion. All designs and code will be released upon paper acceptance. Project website: https://jiannnh.github.io/VecTile/.

infographic.key_insight: VecTile uses passive silicone nubs to convert normal and shear forces into distinguishable pressure patterns, enabling low-cost three-axis tactile sensing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The flexible, 6 mm-thin sensor costs under US$35 for a 4×4 array and provides contact-force feedback for robotic manipulation.
method: Combine a piezoresistive layer with passive silicone nubs.
Validate force-to-pressure transduction using finite element analysis and hardware experiments.
Calibrate force estimates and test transfer from flat to curved configurations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Controlled single-taxel tests over 1–5 N normal force and up to 1.5 N shear force yielded RMSEs of 0.39 N and 0.16 N for normal and shear forces, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Reported force errors come from controlled single-taxel tests; full-array accuracy under simultaneous contacts is not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: VecTile: A Low-Cost Flexible Tactile Array for 3-DoF Force Sensing

title: Sparse-grid discretizations of BGG sequences
authors: Yihanqi Hu, Yuwen Li
abstract: We develop the first tensor-product sparse-grid finite element discretizations of Bernstein--Gelfand--Gelfand (BGG) complexes. Alpert wavelets and their first and second primitives yield compatible hierarchies of discontinuous, continuous, and continuously differentiable piecewise polynomials, that serve as one-dimensional ingredients of BGG sparse-grid finite elements. We construct a bounded commuting sparse-grid projection that yields stable discrete potentials for Hessian, elasticity, and div-div complexes. Under mixed Sobolev regularity, we prove sparse-grid approximation estimates with dimension-independent convergence rates in the number of degrees of freedom. Experiments for a three-dimensional incompatibility problem and a two-dimensional biharmonic problem on an annulus illustrate the efficiency of sparse grids relative to full grids.

infographic.key_insight: Compatible sparse-grid finite elements discretize BGG complexes with stable discrete potentials and dimension-independent convergence rates under mixed Sobolev regularity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports efficient discretizations of elasticity and higher-order mechanics problems with fewer degrees of freedom than full tensor-product grids.
method: Build compatible polynomial hierarchies from Alpert wavelets and their first and second primitives.
Construct a bounded commuting sparse-grid projection for Hessian, elasticity, and div-div complexes.
Prove approximation estimates under mixed Sobolev regularity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on a 3D incompatibility problem and a 2D biharmonic problem on an annulus illustrate efficiency relative to full grids.
infographic.watch_item: The convergence guarantees require mixed Sobolev regularity, which should be checked for problems with singularities or limited smoothness.
infographic.paper_title: Sparse-grid discretizations of BGG sequences
